name: The Nernst Equation
statement: An electrode's voltage shifts from its standard value by the log of the concentrations.
statementAccent: by the log of the concentrations
meaning: The Nernst equation gives the potential of an electrochemical reaction under real conditions from its standard potential and the concentrations, strictly the activities, of the species involved. The potential equals the standard potential minus a term proportional to temperature and to the logarithm of the reaction quotient. It is how the voltage of a cell or electrode responds to the amounts of the reacting species.
mechanism: The equation follows directly from thermodynamics. The Gibbs free energy change of a cell reaction equals minus the number of electrons times the Faraday constant times the potential, and the free energy also equals its standard value plus a term with the gas constant, temperature, and the logarithm of the reaction quotient. Combine the two and divide through, and the Nernst equation emerges. At twenty-five degrees the temperature-dependent prefactor works out so that the potential shifts by about 0.059 volts per unit change in the base-ten logarithm, divided by the number of electrons transferred.

examples.text: An electrode's potential varies with the logarithm of the hydrogen-ion activity, so a measured voltage maps directly to pH — the basis of the pH meter and of ion-selective electrodes generally.

The equilibrium potential of an ion across a cell membrane follows the Nernst form, giving values near minus ninety millivolts for potassium and plus sixty for sodium, from which resting potentials and action potentials are built.
A cell made of identical electrodes in solutions of different concentration produces a voltage predicted purely by the Nernst term, since the standard potentials cancel.

variants.name: The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation
variants.text: The multi-ion generalisation for cell membranes, weighting each ion by its permeability; the single-ion Nernst potential is its limiting case when one ion dominates.

variants.name: The room-temperature form
variants.text: At twenty-five degrees the equation reduces to a shift of about 0.059 volts per decade divided by the number of electrons — convenient, but valid only at that temperature.

whyItMatters: It is the bridge between thermodynamics and electrochemistry, telling how a cell's voltage depends on the concentrations of its species. It underlies potentiometric measurement in chemistry, the electrophysiology of nerves and muscles, the behaviour of batteries and fuel cells, and the study of corrosion — one of the most widely applied relations across the physical and life sciences.

working.text: adjust the standard electrode potential by the Nernst term to find the potential under actual concentrations.
invert the logarithmic relation, as a pH meter does, to get a concentration or activity from a measured potential.

working.lead: Recompute the factor off room temperature
working.text: do not reuse the 0.059-volt figure away from twenty-five degrees; recalculate the temperature-dependent prefactor.

limits: The equation is exact in activities; using concentrations assumes activity coefficients near one, which introduces error in concentrated or high-ionic-strength solutions. It applies at equilibrium, with no net current: under significant current, kinetic limitations and overpotential make real potentials deviate, and it captures no electrode kinetics. As a species' concentration approaches zero the logarithm diverges, so it breaks down at extreme dilution. The convenient room-temperature factor holds only at twenty-five degrees. And a single-ion membrane potential is an idealisation, since real membranes pass several ions at once, for which the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation is needed.
misreadings: Nernst did not win his Nobel Prize for this equation — the 1920 chemistry prize was for his work in thermochemistry, centred on his heat theorem. The resting potential of a cell is close to the potassium equilibrium potential but not equal to it, because sodium and chloride permeabilities shift it, so the multi-ion equation is needed for the true value. And the equation predicts the equilibrium, open-circuit potential, not the delivered voltage of a battery under load, which is lowered by overpotential and resistance.
origin: Derived by the German physical chemist Walther Nernst in 1889, in his habilitation work, linking thermodynamics to electrochemistry; the multi-ion Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz generalisation for membranes came later.
